title: Anton Philips Came for Six Months to Sell His Brother's Lamps
dek: In 1895, after a failed attempt to sell their struggling Eindhoven lamp factory, Frederik Philips sent for his youngest son to sell what Gerard made.

story.event: Bringing in Anton to sell the lamps after losses and a failed sale of the Eindhoven factory
story.summary: Philips & Co, founded in Eindhoven in 1891 by the engineer Gerard Philips and his father Frederik, struggled to make and sell carbon-filament lamps against German competition; after losses in 1893 the family tried in 1894 to sell it but refused the only offer. In January 1895 Frederik brought in his youngest son Anton, 20, for six months to handle sales; Anton travelled by third-class train with a sample case, built 28 agencies within five years and stayed, becoming a partner in 1899 and later head of the company.
paragraphs: In early January 1895 Anton Philips, twenty years old and working at the stock exchange in London, came to Eindhoven at his father's request. He had agreed to stay six months. His brother Gerard, sixteen years older and an engineer, had been making carbon-filament lamps since 1892 in a small factory on the Emmasingel, with money from their father Frederik, a tobacco merchant and banker from Zaltbommel.

The first years had been hard. In 1892 the factory made about 11,000 lamps, many of them failures, and in the opening weeks of 1893 Gerard filled a notebook with experiments on making carbon filaments that came out the same each time. The firm could make neither as many lamps as he had forecast nor sell them at the price he expected; the big German makers dominated the market. According to the company's entry in the International Directory of Company Histories, it lost heavily in 1893, and in 1894 father and son decided to sell. The only offer was one Frederik would not accept, and they chose to risk carrying on rather than sell cheaply.

By late 1894 Gerard had finished the trial stage of production. What the firm lacked was someone to sell. Gerard preferred to stay out of the foreground, his biographer wrote, and Frederik was busy with his bank, so he sent for his youngest son. Anton set out by third-class train with a sample case of lamps, starting in the Netherlands, Belgium and the Ruhr. He later said he took pride in "spending as little money as possible", sometimes spent 21 nights a month on trains and came home bitten by fleas and lice. "But how pleasant it was when you had sold a lot."

The six months did not end. Within five years Anton had built a network of 28 agencies, from Buenos Aires to Yokohama, and opened markets in Russia, Spain and Italy; in April 1899 he became a partner. Gerard kept to the factory, holding, in the museum's rendering, that "When the quality is there, the quantity comes naturally." By 1905 the firm made about four million lamps a year, third in Europe after AEG and Siemens & Halske. Anton ran the company alone from 1922 until 1939.

quote.text: A man hath a body, and that body is confined to a place; but where friendship is, all offices of life are as it were granted to him, and his deputy. For he may exercise them by his friend.
quote.source_title: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral, Project Gutenberg eBook #575
quote.connection: Bacon's point is that a friend lets one person be in two places and do through another what he cannot do himself. Gerard, who avoided the foreground, stayed at the Emmasingel getting the filaments right, while his brother carried the lamps across Europe on night trains.

reflection: The Philips factory did not struggle because Gerard was a poor engineer. It struggled because one man was trying to be both the maker and the seller, and the selling needed someone willing to sleep on trains and talk about the lamps without embarrassment.

You may know this split from your own days: the work you do well at a bench or a desk, and the work of carrying it to people who need convincing. Being one body in one place is not a flaw to be cured by longer hours. It may simply be a reason to ask someone with different gifts to carry part of the load, even for six months.
invitation: Name one task you keep doing badly because it is not your strength, and one person for whom it is. Ask them this week for an hour of help, or only for their advice.

sources.title: Anton Philips (1874-1951)
sources.publisher: Philips Museum, text by Miriam Lengová, Philips Company Archives
sources.supports: Anton, 20, came to Eindhoven in early January 1895 at his father Frederik's request to help his brother Gerard, 16 years older, with the commercial side; he was working at the London stock exchange and agreed to a temporary six-month assignment; the sample case and third-class trains; his quotations about spending as little money as possible and 'But how pleasant it was when you had sold a lot'; 21 nights a month on trains and flea and lice bites; markets in the Netherlands, Belgium, the Ruhr, then Russia, Spain and Italy; 28 agencies within five years from Buenos Aires to Yokohama; Anton director alone after 1922; stepped down in July 1939.

sources.title: Gerard Philips
sources.supports: Founding on 15 May 1891 in a vacant Eindhoven factory; focus on one product, the carbon-filament lamp; Gerard's motto 'When the quality is there, the quantity comes naturally'; Anton joined the sales side in 1895.

sources.title: Report of research: 'Notebook Gerard Philips' (from 1893)
sources.supports: Production in the small factory on the Emmasingel began in 1892; about 11,000 lamps made in 1892 with many failures; Gerard's notebook of 31 January to 6 March 1893 on making reproducible carbon filaments.

sources.title: Philips, Gerard Leonard Frederik (1858-1942)
sources.publisher: A. Heerding, Biografisch Woordenboek van Nederland, Huygens ING
sources.supports: Partnership with his father Frederik, a tobacco and coffee trader, manufacturer and banker, on 15 May 1891; small-scale start to gain experience; trial production finished during 1894; production rising from 400,000 to 4,000,000 lamps a year between 1895 and 1905, third in Europe after AEG and Siemens & Halske; Anton in charge of sales from 1895 and a partner from 1 April 1899; Gerard as manufacturer focused on quality, Anton calling himself a merchant; Gerard avoided putting himself in the foreground; Gerard handed the leadership to Anton on 1 April 1922.

sources.title: N.V. Philips Gloeilampemfabrieken (International Directory of Company Histories)
sources.supports: Frederik, a wealthy tobacco merchant and banker from Zaltbommel, financed the firm; production began in 1892; the firm could not make as many lamps as Gerard forecast nor sell them at the expected price; strong German competition; heavy losses in 1893; the 1894 decision to sell, the only offer unacceptable to Frederik, and the choice to carry on rather than sell too cheaply; Frederik busy with banking and Gerard not a businessman, so Frederik turned to Anton, who joined in early 1895 and won new customers.

sources.title: Philips Light Bulb Factory
sources.supports: Gerard bought a small empty factory on the Emmasingel; the firm focused on the carbon-filament lamp alone; it profited from 1894; yearly production grew twentyfold between 1895 and 1905 to four million lamps, making Philips & Co the third-largest lamp maker in Europe after AEG and Siemens & Halske.

cross_checks.claim: Philips & Co was founded in Eindhoven in May 1891 by Gerard Philips with money from his father Frederik, and production began in 1892.
The early factory struggled: many failed lamps in 1892, output and prices below Gerard's forecast, and strong German competition.
In early 1895 Frederik brought in his youngest son Anton to handle sales.
Trial production ended in 1894 and the firm began to do better from that year.
By 1905 Philips made about four million lamps a year and was third in Europe after AEG and Siemens & Halske.
Gerard's motto was that quantity follows quality.

research_notes: The 1894 attempt to sell the firm rests on a single text: the International Directory of Company Histories entry (also reproduced at referenceforbusiness.com and company-histories.com, which are copies, not independent sources). No independent source naming the buyer or price was found, so the story attributes the sale attempt to that entry and makes no cross-check claim for it. A Russian-language-derived page (stereoindex) repeats the sale story but is not a reliable source and is not cited. Timing tension: Dirk van Delft (Inventing Europe) says Philips profited considerably from 1894 and Heerding (BWN) says trial production ended during 1894, while the IDCH places the decision to sell in 1894 after heavy 1893 losses; these can both be true (a sale considered early in the year, improvement later), so the story says the trial stage was finished by late 1894 and that the firm still lacked a seller. Production figures disagree for 1895: Heerding (BWN) gives 400,000 lamps rising to 4,000,000 a year between 1895 and 1905; van Delft says output grew by a factor of twenty to four million, implying about 200,000 in 1895, which matches Johan Soetens's local-history article (De Oude Flesch, about 200,000 in 1895 and 3 million in 1900). The story uses only the agreed end figure (about four million by 1905) and does not state the 1895 base. The 1892 figure of about 11,000 lamps comes from the Philips Museum and matches Soetens. Anton's arrival: the Philips Museum gives early January 1895; some secondary sites say 1894; the story follows the company archives. The Anton quotations are the Philips Company Archives' English renderings of his recollections; the first is quoted only as a fragment and the museum's own ellipsis is not reproduced. Gerard's motto is quoted in the museum's English translation; Heerding gives it in Dutch. Funding: the slate said 'mixed'; the firm was financed by Frederik Philips, a co-founder, with no outside investors found, so it is marked bootstrapped. Frederik's role is described in BWN as tobacco and coffee trader, manufacturer and banker, and in IDCH as tobacco merchant and banker; the story uses the shorter form. Bacon's essay concerns friendship generally; the Philips brothers are an application by analogy.
